entry.title: The Bitter Lesson and DSD
entry.content:
← All posts

I first started questioning my understanding of The Bitter Lesson when I realized something:

My dad had not exactly started from scratch when he beat me at Go.

I first read the essay in the first year of my PhD, shortly after moving from “traditional robotics” into robot learning. It was remarkably short, but it changed how I thought about the field. Many things we had worked so hard to design might eventually be surpassed by a more general approach that simply learned from enough experience and computation.

The part about Go brought back a childhood memory.

I took Go lessons for two years in primary school. Among my classmates, I was practically unbeatable. Then I taught my dad the rules. Before long, he was beating me convincingly.

I had spent more time studying Go. My teacher had taught me capture techniques, opening patterns, and familiar sequences. My dad knew none of them. Somehow, this self-taught player had demolished my little expert system, carefully packed with human knowledge.

Devastated, I retired.

So when I read The Bitter Lesson years later, my first reaction was: absolutely. I had personally experienced the bitterness in primary school.

Sutton’s argument is about the long run: general methods that can keep using more computation, especially search and learning, tend to outlast approaches built around carefully encoded domain knowledge. 1 It made me wonder how much of our design work was necessary, and how much came from being uncomfortable letting a model learn.

Then, much later, I noticed the missing part of my childhood story.

My dad had never studied those opening patterns. But I had taught him the rules of the game: which moves were legal, how stones were captured, and what counted as winning. Even AlphaGo Zero, which learned without human game records, received a well-formulated problem. It did not first have to inspect a camera feed and discover which moves were legal and which were not. 2

I had not taught my dad how to win. I had already told him what game he was playing.

He could focus on how to play well, because he already knew the rules and what he was trying to achieve.

This story does not refute Sutton’s argument. It does, however, help me distinguish prescribing a solution from choosing how to express a problem.

If a representation makes useful relationships in the data easier to learn, I see no contradiction in studying it while believing in learning.

Letting the model find the answer does not make the way we write the question irrelevant.

This reminds me of a game from my university orientation: ‘How many mosquitoes?’

Someone who knows the rule makes a few gestures, then suddenly asks how many mosquitoes there are. I was completely lost. Was I supposed to count fingers? Claps? Watch which hand moved first?

I did some very serious feature engineering. I also kept getting the answer wrong.

Eventually, someone told me the rule. Everything made sense immediately, and I acquired a new way to annoy other people.

What stayed with me was how many examples I had seen while paying attention to the wrong things. Could I have figured it out alone? Probably, with enough observations and experiments. But the space of possible rules was large, and searching through it without knowing which clues mattered was costly and inefficient.

Giving me the rule gave away the answer. That is not what I want to do for a robot. The question I care about is whether we can make useful relationships easier to see while leaving the behavior itself to be learned.

Data, compute, and robot time all cost something. A robot still has to spend every second of its experience in the physical world. It seems reasonable to ask whether we have accidentally made its learning problem harder than it needs to be.

That is the question behind our recent project, Direction–Scale Decomposition, or DSD: before deciding how to tokenize actions, what exactly are we asking the tokenizer to encode? 3

A vision-language-action model learns to predict robot actions from observations and instructions. In a common discrete-token setup, movements are written as numerical pose increments and converted into tokens.

Those numbers deserve some attention.

Imagine two demonstrations following the same path at different speeds. With a fixed sampling rate, the faster demonstration has larger displacements at each step. Coordinate-wise binning can therefore produce different action tokens even when the direction is unchanged.

Across datasets, different normalization statistics can also map exactly the same physical motion to different tokens.

I picture the robot trying to learn a task while also wondering: ‘Are these movements different, or was this teleoperator in a hurry?’

Token IDs are labels; they do not explicitly show which motions share a direction or how their distances compare. The model has to learn these relationships while also learning the task. A rough analogy is arithmetic in language models: learning patterns of number tokens does not automatically lead to reliable calculation.

Speed and magnitude can matter enormously. A representation should retain that information. But it can also expose what two movements share.

DSD separates a translation into its direction and distance, and a relative rotation into its axis and angle. Magnitudes remain in separate scale channels. The gripper command stays as it is. This happens before tokenization, so we can study the representation with different tokenizers. 34

We have separated ‘which way’ from ‘how far.’ The model still has to learn both.

A longer displacement along the same direction changes the scale without changing the direction target. This property assumes a consistent coordinate convention; DSD does not automatically align different robot frames or controllers.

The geometric information was already present in the original action. DSD makes part of that structure explicit. Before quantization, the decomposition preserves the represented motion.

We evaluated DSD with uniform binning, called BIN, and with the B-spline tokenizer BEAST. Here are the main success-rate comparisons from the paper. Differences are percentage points. 3

The mixed-dataset result is the one that most makes me think about The Bitter Lesson. In our SimplerEnv experiments, adding four datasets to Bridge training reduced BIN’s overall success from 40.0% to 33.0%, while DSD-BIN increased from 40.7% to 43.3%. 3

That is one five-dataset mixture, with gains that vary by task. It is not a scaling law. But it raises a question I find more useful than arguing about whether we should design less: does the action representation affect how much a model benefits from additional data?

If it does, studying representation can help us make better use of scale. The model continues learning from demonstrations; the representation affects how those demonstrations are presented.

This is also what I like about the example of ResNet. Residual learning made deeper networks easier to optimize without supplying a set of rules for recognizing cats. 5 The connection I see with DSD is that a design can make learning easier without prescribing the solution.

A plausible geometric story is not enough to make DSD useful. Our current results leave further questions about action representation open.

What has changed for me since first reading The Bitter Lesson is the question I ask about a design. Does it constrain the learner to follow our preferred solution, or does it help the learner discover relationships in its experience? And does that help survive as we give it more data and computation?

Back when I taught my dad Go, I explained the rules of the game. I still left him to figure out his next move.

He learned that part himself.

Then he used it to beat me.

Paper and demonstrations: see the DSD paper 3 and project page 4.

References

  1. Rich Sutton. The Bitter Lesson.
  2. Google DeepMind. AlphaGo Zero: Starting from scratch.
  3. Duan et al. Direction-Scale Decomposition in Action Representation.
  4. DSD project page and demonstrations.
  5. He et al. Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.

entry.title: a post with tabs
entry.content:
This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

First tabs

To add tabs, use the following syntax:

{% tabs group-name %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-1 %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php
  • js
  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

  • A quote

  • Hipster list

    • brunch
    • fixie
    • raybans
    • messenger bag

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

entry.title: a post with code diff
entry.content:
You can display diff code by using the regular markdown syntax:

```diff
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

Which generates:

diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

But this is difficult to read, specially if you have a large diff. You can use diff2html to display a more readable version of the diff. For this, just use diff2html instead of diff for the code block language:

```diff2html
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

From: Rodrigo Fernandes <rtfrodrigo@gmail.com>
Date: Sat, 15 Oct 2016 13:21:22 +0100
Subject: [PATCH 2/2] Allow uncompiled templates

---
 README.md                 |  3 +++
 src/hoganjs-utils.js      |  7 +++++++
 test/hogan-cache-tests.js | 24 +++++++++++++++++++++++-
 3 files changed, 33 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 132c8a28..46909f25 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -98,6 +98,9 @@ The HTML output accepts a Javascript object with configuration. Possible options
   - `synchronisedScroll`: scroll both panes in side-by-side mode: `true` or `false`, default is `false`
   - `matchWordsThreshold`: similarity threshold for word matching, default is 0.25
   - `matchingMaxComparisons`: perform at most this much comparisons for line matching a block of changes, default is `2500`
+  - `templates`: object with previously compiled templates to replace parts of the html
+  - `rawTemplates`: object with raw not compiled templates to replace parts of the html
+  > For more information regarding the possible templates look into [src/templates](https://github.com/rtfpessoa/diff2html/tree/master/src/templates)

 ## Diff2HtmlUI Helper

diff --git a/src/hoganjs-utils.js b/src/hoganjs-utils.js
index 0dda08d7..b2e9c275 100644
--- a/src/hoganjs-utils.js
+++ b/src/hoganjs-utils.js
@@ -17,6 +17,13 @@
   function HoganJsUtils(configuration) {
     this.config = configuration || {};
     extraTemplates = this.config.templates || {};
+
+    var rawTemplates = this.config.rawTemplates || {};
+    for (var templateName in rawTemplates) {
+      if (rawTemplates.hasOwnProperty(templateName)) {
+        if (!extraTemplates[templateName]) extraTemplates[templateName] = this.compile(rawTemplates[templateName]);
+      }
+    }
   }

   HoganJsUtils.prototype.render = function(namespace, view, params) {
diff --git a/test/hogan-cache-tests.js b/test/hogan-cache-tests.js
index 3bb754ac..a34839c0 100644
--- a/test/hogan-cache-tests.js
+++ b/test/hogan-cache-tests.js
@@ -36,7 +36,7 @@ describe('HoganJsUtils', function() {
       assert.equal(null, result);
     });

-    it('should allow templates to be overridden', function() {
+    it('should allow templates to be overridden with compiled templates', function() {
       var emptyDiffTemplate = HoganJsUtils.compile('<p></p>');

       var config = {templates: {'generic-empty-diff': emptyDiffTemplate}};
@@ -44,5 +44,27 @@ describe('HoganJsUtils', function() {
       var result = hoganUtils.render('generic', 'empty-diff', {myName: 'Rodrigo Fernandes'});
       assert.equal('<p>Rodrigo Fernandes</p>', result);
     });
+
+    it('should allow templates to be overridden with uncompiled templates', function() {
+      var emptyDiffTemplate = '<p></p>';
+
+      var config = {rawTemplates: {'generic-empty-diff': emptyDiffTemplate}};
+      var hoganUtils = new (require('../src/hoganjs-utils.js').HoganJsUtils)(config);
+      var result = hoganUtils.render('generic', 'empty-diff', {myName: 'Rodrigo Fernandes'});
+      assert.equal('<p>Rodrigo Fernandes</p>', result);
+    });
+
+    it('should allow templates to be overridden giving priority to compiled templates', function() {
+      var emptyDiffTemplate = HoganJsUtils.compile('<p></p>');
+      var emptyDiffTemplateUncompiled = '<p>Not used!</p>';
+
+      var config = {
+        templates: {'generic-empty-diff': emptyDiffTemplate},
+        rawTemplates: {'generic-empty-diff': emptyDiffTemplateUncompiled}
+      };
+      var hoganUtils = new (require('../src/hoganjs-utils.js').HoganJsUtils)(config);
+      var result = hoganUtils.render('generic', 'empty-diff', {myName: 'Rodrigo Fernandes'});
+      assert.equal('<p>Rodrigo Fernandes</p>', result);
+    });
   });
 });

entry.title: a post with vega lite
entry.content:
This is an example post with some vega lite code.

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}
```

Which generates:

{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",

        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
